claim: Define the two modes by function (an autonomous pass versus a pass that holds a hypothetical apart), not by speed. Speed, load and accuracy only correlate with the types. Critic papers now read: Melnikoff and Bargh 2018 say the alignment of features has never been measured (16 cells, 2 predicted); Keren and Schul 2009 say a typology needs dichotomy, alignment and separability and none is shown, and offer a many-parts or continuous-depth model; Evans and Stanovich 2013 concede the features are correlates and keep working memory and decoupling as the defining pair. No study tested whether a continuous-depth gate beats a binary gate, so that design choice is open.
agent_test: Compare a gate keyed on a function cue (does the item contain a computation or a candidate to test) against a gate keyed on speed or length cues, at equal tokens, on a mixed item set.

claim: On conflict problems the wrong first answer is mostly one dominant lure, not scattered errors (bat-and-ball: 64.9% intuitive wrong vs 4.8% other wrong; 58% lure vs 6% foils in a 4-option version; 94.9% lure among wrong first responses).
agent_test: For known problem families keep a short list of lure answers. Code flags any attempt whose answer equals a lure and sends it to a check. Measure the lure rate in first-pass samples at equal tokens.

claim: Humans show a response-time and confidence cost on conflict items even when they answer with the lure, read as implicit conflict detection. Boundaries: the mouse-tracking CRT study found no overall conflict response-time cost, and part of the base-rate time effect was attributed to extreme base rates (snippet only).
agent_test: Check whether a cheap model signal (disagreement across 3 short samples, token entropy of the first answer) separates lure-answered from correct items on perturbed CRT-style items. Use it as a gate only if it beats a constant rule at equal tokens.

claim: Some correct answers on conflict problems are already correct in a fast, load-limited first response, and the size depends on task and sample. Re-measured shares of final-correct answers that were first-correct: about 53% on the CRT (28.35% vs 25.33% for 11 vs 01, N=908); 56% and 78% on untrained bat-and-ball controls; about 84% after a short training. The 75-88% figure from the original two-response study (Bago and De Neys 2017) could not be opened and stays unverified. In a 50-item repeated test only 16% had an insight and 23% were correct from the start, and first-correct answers carried a correct justification only 20.7% of the time.
agent_test: Log first-pass accuracy per task family. If a family is already correct on the first pass, use direct mode for it; check the skip loses no accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Explaining the logic of the problem (short training) raised first-response accuracy in humans (+48.3 vs +6.2 points base-rate; +58.3 vs +4.2 conjunction; bat-and-ball +30.0 and +45.7 first-response points vs +11.9 and +6.1 control), while repetition without feedback did not. The effect is family-bound: it carried to bat-and-two-balls items but not to algebra word problems or other CRT-like lure items. The LLM few-shot jump (2% to 92%) used examples of the same task type as the test items. All human results come from the same research group.
agent_test: Store a verified worked example per problem family in memory and place it in the first-pass prompt. Compare against a generic 'think carefully' line at equal tokens.

claim: Cues meant to switch on analytic mode have mostly failed in controlled replications: time pressure on cooperation (intent-to-treat -0.37 points, N=3,596, 21 labs) and disfluent fonts (16 replications, abstract only).
agent_test: Add 'think carefully' or 'be analytic' prefixes to the plain arm and compare at equal tokens. Randomise, and count unfinished items as failures.

claim: Step-by-step reasoning helps mostly on math, symbolic and logic tasks (mean CoT gains 14.2, 12.3, 6.9 points; 56.9 vs 45.5 on those three) and little elsewhere (56.8 vs 56.1). On old davinci-003 it also helped on CRT traps (5% to 28%).
agent_test: Build the S0 gate from structural cues (equals sign, numbers, multi-step calculation). Measure direct vs short-reason vs step-by-step per class at equal tokens and see if the gate recovers most of the best-mode gain.

claim: Forced step-by-step thinking can lower accuracy where deliberation also hurts people (artificial grammar: GPT-4o 87.5% to 64.4% with CoT; o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0% on a subset; face recognition worse for all 6 models) and under distractors with longer reasoning. The human-to-model mapping failed in 3 of 6 tasks, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet was flat on grammar learning.
agent_test: Keep a no-deliberation arm on pattern, perception and distractor-heavy tasks. Compare accuracy at 3 reasoning-length caps at equal total tokens.

claim: Always-slow reasoning wastes tokens on easy items: o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens on '2 plus 3', extra solution rounds added little, easy S1-Bench items were over-thought, and a normal mode was most efficient on 80.52% of GSM8K samples in a tri-mode system.
agent_test: Log the index of the first verified-correct solution. Stop after the first passing S4 check on easy items. Measure tokens saved against accuracy lost on a set with known-easy items.

claim: A model's own remark that a question is easy is not a reliable switch to shorter answers (18 of 23 reasoning models did not shorten). Human confidence is also only weakly tied to accuracy.
agent_test: Compare the model's self-rated difficulty with an external difficulty signal (the plain pass rate of the class) as the S0 trigger at equal tokens.

claim: Older GPT-3 models give the CRT lure far more often than people (80% vs 55%) and newer chat models mostly do not (GPT-4 96% correct, 0% lure). Modified items that break the familiar trick bring failures back (99.1% to 1.5% across 5 LLMs; 95.9% of errors reused the old method; o1-preview 10.0% on principle-changed items, 82.5% of its errors reused the original solution), so success on famous items may be memory. 2025 follow-ups on perturbed famous puzzles agree: with thinking on, o3 59.73%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 58.39%, Claude Sonnet 4 54.36% on 149 perturbations (near-perfect on originals); the puzzle-to-unpuzzle gap is 9.1 points for o3 and up to 54 points for older models. No source tested 2026 models.
agent_test: Test the agent's base model on perturbed CRT-style items before adding any deliberation operator. Add a perturbation check to S4 (mutate numbers or the principle, expect the answer to change) and measure at equal tokens.

claim: Rewriting the input to keep only relevant, unopinionated text before solving lifts accuracy (opinion QA 62.8% to 80.3%, oracle 82.0%; GSM-IC distractors 51.7% to 61.3%). Keeping the original text beside the clean text weakens the gain (74.5%). Evidence is one lab, one model (LLaMA-2-70B-chat for both rewrite and solve), 200 and 100 problems; a search for replications on current models found none.
agent_test: Implement S1 input hygiene in code (move guesses and irrelevant numbers to a marked block). Run the solver with and without the block visible, at equal tokens.

claim: Escalating by code-checked conditions (5 steps without reward, invalid action, final answer, unexpected observation) from a cheap default path to a heavy LLM gave 84.7 vs 33.8-45.3 for always-LLM baselines, at 757 vs 1,856-2,983 tokens per action. The paper has no trigger ablation and no always-slow arm at equal tokens, and its fast-only module scored higher than the gated agent on short tasks (78.68 vs 72.81, ChatGPT backend). In a prompt-based tri-mode system slow mode helped only 3.11% of tasks.
agent_test: Port the four triggers to our impasse detector. Compare always-deliberate vs triggered at equal tokens on a stepwise task set.

claim: No single time course has held across tasks. Mouse tracking on the CRT fits default-interventionist (no pull toward the right option when the lure is chosen). Simple belief-bias logic fits parallel processing. Complex syllogisms fit default-interventionist. Fast-correct responses fit neither cleanly.
agent_test: Do not hard-wire a fast-then-slow order. Test order-free (parallel samples plus code selection) against fast-then-check at equal tokens.

claim: The CRT is not a clean measure of reflection: it carries numeracy (numeric ability, not reflection, predicted framing consistency: b=-0.16 vs b=-0.01), is inflated by prior exposure (t=5.53 on accuracy), and the count of intuitive wrong answers is not a separate trait. Yet it predicts heuristics-and-biases performance beyond intelligence (+11.2% unique variance).
agent_test: Separate 'did it check' (gate) from 'could it compute' (executor). Log both, and test whether swapping the executor for code changes the failure rate at equal tokens.

claim: The causal claim that time pressure or fast decisions make people more cooperative is not supported once random assignment is kept (RRR: -0.37 points, CI -2.60 to 1.86; compliant-only 10.37 vs 15.31 in the original). Selection by compliance (65.9% non-compliance under pressure) explains the pattern. This tests intuition-is-prosocial, not dual-process theory itself.
agent_test: When testing a fast mode, keep unfinished items as failures and randomise assignment of items to arms.

claim: A wrong first answer can come with correct encoding of the relation (recall of 'more than' 69.7% vs 25.4% in wrong reasoners), which challenges pure attribute substitution. The confidence effect was tiny (partial eta squared .02). The original substitution account was not opened.
agent_test: Compare restating the task (S1) against supplying a method hint (O6) on items where the first attempt used the wrong method. See which fixes more errors at equal tokens.

claim: A short instruction suffix flips an LLM between writing steps and answering briefly (CoT rate 97% to 0% for ChatGPT-3.5, 84% to 0% for GPT-4), so the fast/slow switch is mostly an output-style toggle that code can control. GPT-4 correct fell 95% to 88% when told to be brief.
agent_test: Set mode in code by choosing a prompt template per class, and compare templates at equal tokens.

claim: Plan with the model, but execute symbolic steps in a program: plan plus a tool solver beat plan plus CoT, and a symbolic solver beat CoT. Search with evaluation (Tree of Thoughts) lifted Game of 24 from 4% to 74% with GPT-4 (model self-evaluation, which G5 distrusts).
agent_test: On arithmetic and constraint slots, replace the model's text computation with code. Compare against CoT at equal tokens, including code-run cost.

claim: Repeated practice without outside feedback does not de-bias (61% of 62 people stayed biased over 50 items), and practised routes change the default (experience moderator in cooperation games, post hoc). Corrections need an external signal.
agent_test: Run the agent twice on the same family, with and without real-output feedback. Compare second-run first-pass accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Disagreement across a model's own samples is a better error signal than its stated confidence on older models (GPT-4 Brier .116 entropy and .119 agreement vs .154 and .181 stated; 3 to 5 samples already help), but agreement is weak and over-confident on a current frontier model: gpt-4.1 had agreement of 0.8 or more on 77% of GPQA entries and was wrong on 48% of them, and a confidence-routed cascade lost to always using the mid-tier model. Nobody tested it against a plain class pass rate on perturbed trap items, where all samples may share the lure.
agent_test: On perturbed items, draw 3 short samples per item. Compare three rules at equal tokens for predicting a wrong first answer: sample disagreement, stated uncertainty, and the family's running pass rate. Report AUROC and the accuracy of the routed result.

claim: A gate that reads only the task text and picks a short or long mode can recover most of the long-mode gain on maths at lower cost (7B: 62.8% at 5,405 tokens vs 64.6% at 7,617 for always-long and 46.0% at 1,079 for always-short; a random 25/75 mix gave 58.9% at 5,918; a BERT classifier gave 60.7% at 6,021). A three-way mode (none, short, long) is learnable and cut length 41% at 0.782 vs 0.796 accuracy. All of this is maths with small distilled models; no mixed set with pattern, perception or distractor items was tested and no hand-written structural rule was compared.
agent_test: Build a mixed set (arithmetic, multi-step word problems, grid pattern, perceptual match, distractor items). Compare always-direct, always-steps, a hand rule (numbers, equals sign, multi-step cue, known family) and the family pass-rate rule at equal total tokens.

claim: At equal total thinking tokens on hard maths and GPQA, several parallel attempts stopped early and voted beat waiting for all of them at low and medium budgets (short-3@k +2% at 80k tokens for QwQ-32B, about +4% at 100k for R1-670B), and the shortest chain within a question is up to 34.5 points more accurate than the longest. Independent parallel samples also beat sequential refinement at the same number of solutions. No test fixes total tokens for one long attempt versus 3 to 4 short capped attempts, split by problem class.
agent_test: For each problem class, give the same total token budget to (a) one long attempt, (b) 3 short independent attempts plus code selection, (c) 4 short attempts with early stop. Report accuracy per class.

claim: Asking for a brief answer does not guarantee a first pass without reasoning: with thinking switched off DeepSeek-V4-Flash still showed visible reasoning in 99.9% of open-ended answers, and strict answer-only prompts on open-ended tasks cut mean accuracy by about 15 points. Boolean tasks comply best (80 to 100% answer-only). Any test of a direct arm must log the text before the answer.
agent_test: Enforce the fast route in code (hard token cap, answer parsed from a fixed slot) and log how often visible reasoning appears before the answer.

claim: Worked examples fix the first pass inside a family but not across families. Humans: a short explanation of bat-and-ball raised first-response accuracy and lasted at least two months, but did not transfer to algebra word problems or other CRT-like lure items. LLM: same-type examples took GPT-3-davinci-003 from 2% to 92% (CRT type 2), 12% to 92% (type 3) and 0% to about 78% (type 1, 30 examples). No source tested held-out principle variants with a verified example in the prompt on a current model.
agent_test: For one family, put a verified worked example in the first-pass prompt. Test on (a) numbers-changed variants, (b) principle-changed variants, (c) a different family. Compare with a generic careful-thinking line at equal tokens.

claim: Whether a task where thinking hurts people also hurts models follows a pattern that was found after the fact: the rule held for statistical rule learning, face recognition and learning with exceptions, and failed where the model has trained logic that people lack (CoT lifted GPT-4o from 53.2% to 93.9% on logical inconsistency), lacks motor priors (no change on tilting glasses) or has far more working memory (CoT helped on apartment choice). The pattern was not predicted in advance and is untested on new tasks.
agent_test: Pick 3 of our own pattern or perception task classes and 3 reasoning classes. Run direct vs steps at equal tokens. Check whether the human-harm rule plus the three exceptions predicts the sign of the effect.

claim: A retry that sees its earlier answer explores less than an independent retry: independent parallel samples beat sequential refinement at the same number of solutions on AIME 2025 for three model families, and aggregation and context length were ruled out as the cause.
agent_test: After a flagged first answer, compare a retry that sees the first answer against a retry with fresh context, at equal tokens, on items with a known lure.
